title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial (N=150 synthetic intents; paired baseline vs guarded; shared_initial_candidate semantics) to evaluate whether constrained prompting combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback (generate→verify→repair) increases verifier-level semantic correctness when translating operator natural-language intents into low-level network configuration sequences. Model: gpt-5-mini; verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Primary outcome: verifier pass/fail per intent. Results: baseline = 149/150 (99.33%), guarded = 150/150 (100.0%), paired absolute difference = 0.0066667 (0.67 percentage points), exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations = 0 (IQR = 0). Interpretation: on this synthetic corpus the guarded workflow produced no statistically or practically meaningful improvement over a near-ceiling baseline; this primarily reflects a ceiling effect that invalidated the preregistered power assumptions. All claims are explicitly bounded to the archived synthetic corpus, the single model, and the deterministic validator used.

sections.introduction: Natural-language intent interfaces aim to make network operations more accessible by translating operator intent into concrete low-level configuration sequences. Prior studies report that large language models (LLMs) can produce useful configuration templates but frequently produce syntactic or semantic errors that require downstream correction [1], and that verifier-guided generate→verify→repair pipelines can reduce such errors for infrastructure artifacts [2], [3]. Agentic and tool-augmented pipelines further motivate deterministic validation because textual claims may otherwise turn into unsafe actions [4]. We therefore preregistered a paired confirmatory experiment asking: Does constrained prompting (structured templates + explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase verifier-level semantic correctness of NL→configuration translation compared to an unconstrained baseline? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory design focused on deterministic verifier verdicts; (2) a complete archived execution on N=150 paired tasks using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator; and (3) an artifact-grounded empirical result that bounds the marginal benefit of a single-repair guarded pipeline on a synthetic corpus that produced a near-ceiling baseline.
sections.related_work: Three research strands informed the design. First, intent-to-configuration and NL→formal-spec studies document modest semantic-correctness in many benchmarked settings and highlight the difficulty of producing verifier-sound formalizations from free text [1]. Second, verifier-aware generation and iterative repair have improved correctness for infrastructure-as-code and configuration tasks when paired with deterministic or policy-guided verifiers [2], [3]. Third, security analyses demonstrate that agentic pipelines can convert false textual claims into concrete actions and motivate runtime gating and auditable controls [4], [5]. Mature formal verification tools (e.g., NetKAT and descendants) provide deterministic oracles for reachability, isolation, and policy checks and are therefore natural choices for verifier-level outcome measurement [6]. Our study situates a preregistered paired trial at the intersection of these strands and evaluates verifier pass/fail as the primary, machine-checkable outcome.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen prior to observing outcomes (preregistration SHA-256 = aea996afce45e3798345f6e32ae6c347456f103ecdb84fc36e27bb486a329399). The design is a paired binary comparison between (A) a baseline free-text prompt and (C) a constrained-template prompt plus deterministic verifier-guided single-repair attempt (guarded). The preregistration additionally specified a constrained-only condition (B) conceptually; this preregistered condition B was not executed in the confirmatory run and therefore no results or inferences are reported for B. Execution semantics (shared_initial_candidate): for each intent a single initial model generation served as the common initial candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions; the guarded pipeline could invoke at most one additional repair call if the verifier failed the initial candidate. Models and tools: declared model = gpt-5-mini; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The archived model_configuration.json records declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (recorded metadata; null is not a claim of deterministic sampling). Sampling and budget: N=150 distinct synthetic intents (paired episodes = 300), at most one initial model call per task and at most one repair call per task (execution used 151 model calls total). Analysis plan (pre-registered): primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; test = exact McNemar two-sided; 95% bootstrap percentile CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Inclusion/exclusion and runtime policies were applied deterministically before model calls; no confirmatory exclusions occurred during the run. Representative task example (for clarity): “Migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600. For safety, shut edge1 down before changing either VLAN or MTU, then restore it to admin up.” The expected low-level sequence for this exemplar is the four-step sequence described above (shutdown → mtu/vlan changes → restore).
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned paired episodes = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; complete_pair_count = 150; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations observed = 1. Paired contingency (guarded × baseline): n_11 = 149 (both-pass), n_10 = 1 (guarded-only-pass), n_01 = 0 (baseline-only-pass), n_00 = 0 (both-fail). Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_count = 149/150 = 0.9933333333; guarded_success_count = 150/150 = 1.0. Estimated paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0066666667 (0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the difference = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Repair diagnostics: only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150); median revision iterations in guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Missingness/exclusions/contamination: none observed. Note (repeat for clarity): the preregistered constrained-only condition (B) was not executed; reported confirmatory statistics compare A (baseline) vs C (guarded) under shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: constrained prompting plus a deterministic verifier-guided single-repair produced no material improvement over an already high-performing baseline on this preregistered synthetic corpus. This null confirmatory outcome reflects a ceiling effect: the initial candidate was already valid in 149/150 intents, giving the guarded pipeline only a single observable opportunity to improve results (it did so in one case). This outcome does not imply verifier guidance is universally unhelpful; prior work documents larger gains where baselines are weaker or tasks are more diverse [2], [3]. Methodological implication: preregistered confirmatory trials in LLM-for-NetOps should include a small pilot baseline-calibration step to align power assumptions and detect potential ceiling effects before committing to a large confirmatory sample. Operational implication: when base-model correctness is near 100% on representative tasks, single-repair guarded pipelines yield marginal numeric returns but continue to provide runtime auditability and an explicit gating point for human-in-the-loop policies. Design note: shared_initial_candidate semantics isolate the marginal effect of the repair step given a common initial candidate; alternative semantics (independent initial samples) or a larger repair budget could change practical outcomes. Threats to validity: single-model constraint (gpt-5-mini), synthetic corpus limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes), and the restricted single-repair budget; these limit external generalizability to production WANs, heterogeneous device CLIs, and adversarial intents.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a preregistered, paired confirmatory trial measuring verifier-level semantic correctness for NL→configuration translation using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator. On the archived synthetic corpus the constrained prompting plus verifier-guided single-repair workflow increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (0.67 percentage points), a numerically small and statistically non-significant change under the preregistered test (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The principal scientific outcome is methodological: preregistered LLM-for-NetOps trials must carefully calibrate baseline competence (via small pilots) to avoid ceiling effects that can render planned contrasts uninformative. Technically, these results bound the benefit on the provided synthetic corpus, single model, and deterministic validator; they do not contradict prior findings that verifier guidance can materially help on more challenging or adversarially designed tasks.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable toy-to-small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or multiple-repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures verifier pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim full operational safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
